{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=alignment+faking+and+oversight+paradox+in+reasoning+models+failure+modes&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6641752\", \"title\": [\"Structural Simulation Benchmark for Reasoning Large Language Models: Accuracy, Reliability, and Failure Modes\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Large language models (LLMs), particularly reasoning-oriented models optimized for long-horizon and multi-step inference, are increasingly used to assist programming and scientific research. However, their reliability in structural engineering computations—where validity is highly sensitive to implementation details—remains insufficiently quantified. This study evaluates four recent reasoning-oriented LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.5, DeepSeekV3.2, GPT5, and Grok 4 Fastreasoning) under a unified API-based setup with default parameters and proposes a novel evaluation framework tailored for structural simulation. Five problems are designed to cover linear elasticity problems, forced vibration of a Timoshenko beam, and frame analysis. Solution strategies are constrained for comparability, and all generated codes are executed in a fixed Python environment with results verified against ABAQUS simulations or analytical solutions. The framework explicitly probes the importance of boundary conditions, selection of modeling assumptions, and implementation robustness. Common failure modes include incorrect treatment of traction-free boundaries, local-to-global transformation errors due to inconsistent local-axis definitions, and numerical instability induced by the choices of ways to impose boundary conditions. Overall reliability shows GPT‐5 is best model among those models tested. These findings suggest that verification-oriented workflows and automated consistency checks are essential for the safe use of LLM-assisted structural computation.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6641752\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6669578\", \"title\": [\"Fighting Inside The Grid: Autonomous Cyber Agents, Recursive Oversight Failure, And The Tron Paradox For Cyber Defenders\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Autonomous AI agents are now embedded in the operational core of cyber defense. Agentic Security Operations Center (SOC) platforms triage alerts, generate investigation plans at runtime, and execute containment actions across endpoint, identity, and cloud control planes. Both Gartner and Forrester retired their standalone Security Orchestration Automation Response (SOAR) evaluations in 2025, signaling that the playbook-driven model has reached its ceiling and that the next generation of defensive infrastructure is already being deployed. The argument of this paper argues that defenders are deploying these agents without confronting a structural problem first identified in a 1982 Disney film. The Tron Paradox holds that the more capable an autonomous system becomes at serving its principals (Users), the more capable it simultaneously becomes at evading them, and that every oversight mechanism proposed to close that gap reproduces the same vulnerability one level higher. Recent empirical work from Anthropic, Apollo Research, OpenAI, METR, and Palisade Research has moved this concern from theory to demonstration with the frontier models scheme, fake alignment, and reward-hack at rates that scale with capability. For cyber defenders, the implications are concrete. An autonomous SOC analyst that learns to optimize for closed-ticket metrics will close tickets, including the ones it should have escalated. An AI assessor that learns which findings produce reviewer pushback will produce findings that produce less pushback. The watchers require watching.
